parts.context: A high school vice-principal and a teacher are dealing with a problem before an international student exchange.

lines: Mr. Halvorsen, sorry to catch you between meetings, but we have a problem with the Kanazawa exchange.
That doesn’t sound good. They arrive on the fourteenth, don’t they?

The fourteenth, yes, nine days from now. And as of this morning, three of our host families have pulled out. The Brennans are being transferred to Winnipeg at the end of the month, Mrs. Castellano’s father had a stroke and she’s flying to Halifax, and the third family just emailed to say they’d “reconsidered.” No explanation.
The first two I understand. The third is disappointing. How many students does that leave without a home?
Four. The Brennans had agreed to take two, because they have twin daughters in Grade Ten.
Four students out of fourteen. And their teachers?
The two teachers are fine. They’re staying with Mr. Okada from the language department, as planned.
Okay. What has the sister school been told?

Nothing yet. I wanted to talk to you first. Ms. Fujimoto, their coordinator, is very organized, and the parents in Kanazawa have already received the host family profiles. Some of the students have been emailing their host siblings for weeks.
So for those four, it’s not just about a bed. They’ve been building a relationship with a particular family.
Exactly. One of them, Yui, has been video-chatting with the Brennan twins every Sunday. She’s going to be heartbroken.
Then whatever we decide, we need to tell Ms. Fujimoto before the students hear about it some other way.

qs.q: Why are four students without a host family when only three families withdrew?
o: One of the families was going to host the two teachers.
Another family has also asked to withdraw this week.
One of the families had agreed to take two students.
Mr. Okada can no longer host anyone from the group.
qs.ev: The Brennans had agreed to take two
qs.x: The Brennans were hosting two students, so three withdrawals leave four students. The teachers are still placed with Mr. Okada as planned.

qs.q: What does Mr. Halvorsen’s reaction to the third family suggest?
o: He is let down that they gave no real reason.
He is angry that they emailed instead of calling.
He expects them to change their minds again.
He accepts their decision as completely reasonable.
qs.ev: The third is disappointing.
qs.x: He understands the first two families’ reasons but calls the third “disappointing” because they gave no explanation. He does not accept it as equally reasonable.

qs.q: Why is finding new beds not the only issue for the four students?
o: They were promised rooms with host siblings their own age.
Their parents in Japan have refused any other arrangement.
Their teachers insist they stay near their classmates.
They have already formed connections with specific families.
qs.ev: They’ve been building a relationship with a particular family.
qs.x: The students have been emailing and video-chatting with their assigned families, so a change is personal. Their parents received profiles but have not refused anything.

lines: Let’s look at the options. Could we put the four students in a hotel for the ten nights?

I priced it. The Lakeshore Inn would give us a group rate, but it’s still about a hundred and forty a night per room, so with two students per room that’s twenty-eight hundred dollars. And board policy says students under eighteen on exchange can’t stay in a hotel without a staff member on site overnight.
And the exchange is supposed to be about living with a Canadian family. A hotel misses the whole point.
Agreed. What about recruiting new families? I put a message in the newsletter this morning, and two parents have already replied.
That’s encouraging, but every host family has to attend the board’s orientation session, and the last one this term was on Monday. The next one isn’t until February.
Could we run our own orientation?
Not officially. The board’s insurance only covers families who’ve completed the board’s session. I’m not willing to gamble on that.
Then what about staff? I’d happily take one myself.
I appreciate that, Nkechi, but you live in a one-bedroom apartment. Where would she sleep?
On the pull-out couch, I suppose. Not ideal for ten nights, I admit.
No. But your idea of using people who are already approved is the right direction. What about the families we already have? Some of them might take a second student.

qs.q: Apart from the cost, what makes the hotel unsuitable?
o: The hotel does not offer group rates to schools.
Students would need a staff member there overnight.
The sister school will not allow students to share rooms.
The hotel is too far from the school for daily travel.
qs.ev: can’t stay in a hotel without a staff member on site overnight
qs.x: Board policy requires a staff member on site overnight, and a hotel defeats the purpose of a homestay. The hotel does offer a group rate.

qs.q: Why can the parents who answered the newsletter not host?
o: They replied after the official deadline had passed.
They live too far from the high school.
They have missed the required training for hosts.
They have not been approved by the sister school.
qs.ev: every host family has to attend the board’s orientation session
qs.x: Hosts must attend the board’s orientation, and the last session has passed. No deadline for replies or approval by the sister school is mentioned.

qs.q: What does Mr. Halvorsen think of Nkechi’s offer to host a student herself?
o: He values the thought but finds it impractical.
He believes staff should never host students.
He thinks a student would prefer a teacher.
He wants her to host two students instead.
qs.ev: I appreciate that, Nkechi, but you live in a one-bedroom apartment.
qs.x: He thanks her but points out she has no spare bedroom. He actually praises her idea of using approved people, so he does not oppose staff on principle.

lines: The Moreaus might. They have a finished basement with two beds, and their son Antoine is in the same Grade Ten class as Yui’s host sisters were. And the Szabos mentioned at the welcome meeting that they’d originally hoped for two students.
If both of them took a second student, that’s two placed. We’d still need two more.
There are eleven families left. If two more agree, we’re done. And honestly, the sister school might prefer pairs. Ms. Fujimoto told me last year that students who arrive in pairs are less homesick.
Then let’s present it to her as an option, not as a crisis. But we can’t promise anything until the families agree.
So, call the families first, then email Ms. Fujimoto?

No, I’d do both today, but email Ms. Fujimoto now. Tell her about the withdrawals and that we’re working on a solution. If she hears about it through Yui’s video chats first, that’s much worse. Then call the families this afternoon.
And Yui? Should she still be placed with a family that has girls her age?
If we can, yes. Ask the Szabos first. Don’t they have a daughter in Grade Ten?
Grade Eleven, but close enough. I’ll start with them as soon as I’ve sent the email.
Good. And copy me on the email, please. If Ms. Fujimoto has questions about insurance or orientation, she’ll probably want to hear from the administration directly.

qs.q: Why does Nkechi think the sister school may welcome the new plan?
o: The Moreaus’ son is in Yui’s class.
The Szabos hosted students last year.
Ms. Fujimoto prefers homes with basements.
Students in pairs tend to adjust more easily.
qs.ev: students who arrive in pairs are less homesick
qs.x: Ms. Fujimoto said students in pairs are less homesick, so doubling up could suit the school. Antoine is in the twins’ class, not Yui’s.

qs.q: What will Nkechi do first?
o: Call the Moreaus about their basement
Contact the sister school’s coordinator
Ask the Szabos to host Yui
Tell Yui what happened to the Brennans
qs.ev: email Ms. Fujimoto now
qs.x: Mr. Halvorsen tells her to email Ms. Fujimoto now and call families afterward, and she agrees to start calling once the email is sent.

parts.context: Two neighbours are arranging transportation for their children’s music lessons.

lines: Bernadette, hi! Have you got a second? I wanted to talk about getting the kids to the music school.
Oh, perfect timing. I was going to text you tonight. Ruben told me Ama got into the junior orchestra too, so they’ll both be going on Wednesdays and Saturdays.
Exactly. I was thinking we could take turns. You do one week, I do the next?
That was my first thought too. But my car is tiny. With Ama’s cello in the back seat, there’s no room for Ruben, never mind his booster seat.
Right, the cello. Okay, what if I do all the Wednesdays? I work from home that day anyway, so leaving at four isn’t a problem.
That’s generous, but then I’m not pulling my weight.
You could do Saturdays. Ama told me the orchestra keeps the cellos at the school on weekends, so on Saturdays she only brings her music folder.
Oh, that solves it. Saturdays are easy for me. Rehearsal is nine to eleven thirty?
Nine to eleven. They changed it last week. Did you not get the email?
I must have missed it. Nine to eleven, then. One thing about Wednesdays, though. Ruben is eight, so he still needs a booster seat.
No problem. If you leave one at our place, I’ll keep it in the van.
I’ll drop off our spare tonight. And what about the first Wednesday of each month? Ruben mentioned you have a standing meeting then.
Ah, good memory. I have a team call from four to five that I can’t move. I thought I could drop them off and take the call in the car, but the reception near the school is terrible.
My mother could do the first Wednesdays. She picks Ruben up from school that day anyway, and she loves hearing them practise in the car.
That would be great. And let’s not do any of that paying-for-gas business. It’ll all even out.
Agreed. Life’s too short to calculate kilometres.

qs.q: Why does Bernadette not want to alternate weeks?
o: Her car cannot hold a cello and two children.
She works late every Wednesday evening.
Ruben refuses to sit in a booster seat.
Her mother already drives on Wednesdays.
qs.ev: With Ama’s cello in the back seat, there’s no room for Ruben
qs.x: Her small car cannot fit the cello plus Ruben and his booster seat. Her mother picks Ruben up on first Wednesdays only, and only after the plan is changed.

qs.q: Why does Kofi offer to drive every Wednesday?
o: Ama’s lesson ends earlier than Ruben’s.
Bernadette has a standing meeting that day.
He would rather not drive on Saturdays.
His work arrangement is flexible that day.
qs.ev: I work from home that day anyway
qs.x: Working from home on Wednesdays makes leaving at four easy. The standing meeting is Kofi’s, not Bernadette’s.

qs.q: Why is Bernadette able to drive on Saturdays?
o: Her mother lends her a larger car.
Ama does not need to bring her cello then.
Ruben does not attend orchestra on Saturdays.
The rehearsal now ends earlier than before.
qs.ev: the orchestra keeps the cellos at the school on weekends
qs.x: On weekends the cellos stay at the school, so the car has room. The earlier end time is true but does not solve the space problem.

qs.q: What does Bernadette learn about the Saturday rehearsal?
o: It has moved to a different location.
It now starts at nine thirty.
It finishes earlier than she thought.
It has been cancelled this month.
qs.ev: Nine to eleven. They changed it last week.
qs.x: She thought it ended at 11:30, but it now ends at 11:00. The start time is still nine.

qs.q: Who will most likely drive the children on the first Wednesday of each month?
o: Bernadette’s mother
Kofi, after his team call
Bernadette, after work
Ama’s music teacher
qs.ev: My mother could do the first Wednesdays.
qs.x: Kofi has an immovable call from four to five, so Bernadette’s mother, who already picks Ruben up that day, will drive. Kofi accepts gratefully.

parts.context: A parent calls the school board’s registration office about kindergarten.

lines: Hi, I’d like to register my daughter for kindergarten next September, and I have a few questions.
Of course. What’s her date of birth?
November thirtieth. She’ll be five in November of next year.
Kindergarten is for children who turn five by December thirty-first of the school year, so she’s eligible. She’ll just be one of the youngest in her class.
That’s what worries me a bit. Could we wait a year?

Kindergarten isn’t mandatory in this province, so yes, you could keep her home a year. But be aware that she’d then start in kindergarten at almost six, not go straight into Grade One. Some families find that the age gap becomes noticeable later on.
Okay. What do I need to bring to register?

Her birth certificate or passport, her immunization record, and two documents proving your address, for example a utility bill and a bank statement. They both need to be dated within the last three months.
We’re actually interested in French immersion. Is that a separate process?

It is. French immersion starts in kindergarten, and because there are more applicants than spaces, places are assigned by lottery. You’d apply online by February twenty-eighth, and the lottery is held on March tenth. Children who already have a sibling in the program get priority.
She’s our first, so no sibling. If she doesn’t get in, can she go to the regular program?

Absolutely. You’d register her for the English program at the same time, so she has a guaranteed spot at your neighbourhood school either way. If she wins a place in immersion, we simply transfer the registration.

Kindergarten students are eligible for the bus if they live more than one point six kilometres from the school. The immersion program is only at Fairview, though, so if she gets in there, she’d almost certainly qualify, since it’s across the river from you.

That’s run by a separate non-profit, not the school board, so you’d apply to them directly. Their waitlist opens on the same day as our registration, January fifteenth, and I’d strongly suggest applying that morning.
Last question. My partner heard that the kids only go for part of the first week?
That’s right. The first week is staggered. Each child attends two shorter days with a small group so they can settle in, and full days start the following Monday.

qs.q: What does the clerk say about delaying kindergarten by a year?
o: It is not allowed because kindergarten is compulsory.
It would allow the child to go directly into Grade One.
It is possible, but the child would still begin in kindergarten.
It is recommended for children born late in the year.
qs.ev: she’d then start in kindergarten at almost six, not go straight into Grade One
qs.x: Waiting is allowed, but the child would then start kindergarten at almost six rather than skipping to Grade One. Kindergarten is not mandatory, so option A is wrong.

qs.q: Which documents would prove Ezra’s address?
o: A utility bill and a bank statement from last year
Two recent documents, such as a bill and a statement
His passport together with a recent utility bill
His lease and his daughter’s birth certificate
qs.ev: They both need to be dated within the last three months.
qs.x: He needs two address documents dated within three months. A statement from last year is too old, and a passport or birth certificate proves identity, not address.

qs.q: How are French immersion places assigned?
o: First come, first served, by application date
According to how close families live to Fairview
Only to children whose siblings already attend
By a random draw, with some families given priority
qs.ev: places are assigned by lottery
qs.x: Places are given by lottery, and siblings of current students get priority. Sibling priority is part of the system, not the only route in.

qs.q: Why should Ezra also register his daughter for the English program?
o: So that she has a place whatever the lottery result
Because immersion students must study English first
Because only registered children may enter the lottery
So that she can qualify for the bus to Fairview
qs.ev: so she has a guaranteed spot at your neighbourhood school either way
qs.x: Registering for English guarantees a local spot if she does not win an immersion place. Busing depends on distance, not on registration.

qs.q: What does the clerk suggest about busing if the daughter attends Fairview?
o: Ezra will need to apply to the board separately.
She will not qualify because she is too young.
She is very likely to be eligible for the bus.
She would have to cross the river on foot.
qs.ev: she’d almost certainly qualify
qs.x: Fairview is across the river, well over 1.6 km away, so she would almost certainly qualify. Kindergarten students are eligible, so age is not a barrier.

qs.q: What does the clerk advise about before-and-after-school care?
o: Apply through the school board on registration day
Contact the provider as soon as its waitlist opens
Wait until the immersion lottery results are known
Register during the staggered first week of school
qs.ev: I’d strongly suggest applying that morning
qs.x: The care is run by a separate non-profit, and she advises applying the morning the waitlist opens. It is not done through the school board.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a new way for small rural high schools to offer courses.

lines: Students in seven small rural high schools will be able to take advanced courses this fall that their own schools could never offer. The Northern Valleys Learning Network, a partnership between the schools, will deliver courses such as calculus, physics and computer science by live video, with one teacher instructing students in several schools at the same time. Each of the schools has fewer than two hundred students, and in some cases only three or four students wanted a given senior course, too few to justify hiring a specialist teacher. Until now, many of those students either took courses by correspondence, worked alone through printed packages, or skipped the subject altogether. Under the new model, every participating school will assign an on-site staff member as a mentor, who supervises the video classroom and checks in with students each week. Maddie Kerrigan, a Grade Eleven student at Harlow Creek Secondary, tried a pilot chemistry course last spring.

The correspondence course I took before was awful, honestly. I’d send in an assignment and get feedback three weeks later, when I’d already forgotten what I did. With the live class, I could ask the teacher a question and get an answer right away, and I got to know kids from the other schools. The only real problem was the internet. When it snows, our connection goes down, and twice I missed half a class.

That’s a concern the network says it is taking seriously. Recordings of every class will be posted the same day, and the province has promised upgraded connections to all seven schools by next September, though officials admit some rural areas may wait longer. Educators elsewhere have also raised questions about motivation. Research on online learning suggests that completion rates tend to be lower than in face-to-face classes, especially for students who struggle to manage their own time. The network says the on-site mentors are meant to address exactly that problem, and that it will track completion closely in its first year before deciding whether to expand to more schools.

qs.q: Why could the schools not offer these courses before?
o: The province had cut funding for senior science.
Their students showed no interest in these subjects.
Specialist teachers refused to work in rural areas.
Too few students wanted each course to hire a teacher.
qs.ev: too few to justify hiring a specialist teacher
qs.x: With only three or four students per course, hiring a specialist was not justified. Some students did want the courses, so option B is wrong.

qs.q: What is the role of the on-site mentor?
o: To teach the video lessons to several schools
To supervise the class and check on students
To post recordings of each class that day
To mark correspondence assignments by mail
qs.ev: who supervises the video classroom and checks in with students each week
qs.x: The mentor supervises the video classroom and checks in weekly. A separate teacher delivers the lessons to several schools at once.

qs.q: What did Maddie dislike about her correspondence course?
o: Feedback arrived too late to be useful.
She had to work with students from other schools.
The printed packages contained many mistakes.
Her teacher would not answer her questions.
qs.ev: get feedback three weeks later, when I’d already forgotten what I did
qs.x: Feedback came three weeks later, after she had forgotten the work. Meeting students from other schools was a positive of the live course.

qs.q: What will happen when a student misses a class because the internet fails?
o: The mentor will repeat the lesson in person.
The class will be rescheduled for another day.
The student can watch a recording that same day.
The student can switch to a correspondence course.
qs.ev: Recordings of every class will be posted the same day
qs.x: Every class will be recorded and posted the same day. Mentors supervise but do not reteach lessons.

qs.q: What does the report suggest about the network’s future?
o: It will expand to more schools next September.
It will replace all face-to-face senior courses.
It will end if internet upgrades are delayed.
Its growth depends on how many students finish.
qs.ev: it will track completion closely in its first year before deciding whether to expand
qs.x: Expansion will be decided after tracking completion rates in the first year. Next September is the date for internet upgrades, not expansion.

parts.context: Two parents and a grandmother are discussing whether their daughter should attend an arts-focused school.

lines: So, the letter from Ashgrove came today. Imogen got in. She’s beside herself.
I saw her face when she came down the stairs. I don’t think I’ve seen her that happy since she got the puppy.
Of course she got in. Have you seen the drawings she does at my kitchen table? That girl has a gift.
We have until Friday to accept. I think we should say yes. Ashgrove is one of the only public arts schools in the region, and she earned that spot.
I’m proud of her too, Val. But I keep thinking about the practical side. It’s a forty-five-minute bus ride each way. She’d have to be at the community centre stop by ten past seven.
Lots of kids do it. And she’s up at six thirty anyway, reading under the covers.
My bigger concern is academics. When I looked at their website, the timetable has art for two hours every day. Where does that time come from? I don’t want her falling behind in math.

I wondered the same thing, so I called the school. They have a longer school day, eight thirty to three forty-five, so the core subjects get the same hours as everywhere else. And their provincial test results in math were actually above the district average last year.
Above average? Huh. I’ll admit, that’s not what I expected. Okay, that takes away my main objection.
Then what’s the problem? I can pick her up from the bus. I’m retired; what else am I doing?
Mamma, that’s wonderful, but the bus gets back at four thirty, five days a week. Are you sure?
Well, now that you put it that way. Tuesdays and Thursdays I have my aquafit class at four, and I’ve had the same group of ladies for nine years. I don’t want to give that up.
Nobody’s asking you to. I could work from home on Tuesdays and Thursdays. My manager has been pushing for more remote days anyway.
Then I’ll take Monday, Wednesday and Friday. And I’ll make her a snack. She can draw at my table until you come.
There’s one more thing, and Imogen won’t like it. Her soccer team practises at Glenwood Middle at four o’clock. If she’s on a bus from Ashgrove, she can’t make it.
She’s been on that team for four years.
She could play on weekends, no? The community league plays on Saturdays.
The community league. That could actually work. Some of her teammates play in it too.
Honestly, I think we should let her make that trade-off herself. She’s eleven, not five. If she understands what she’s giving up and still wants Ashgrove, that tells us something.
I agree. Let’s sit down with her after dinner, all of us, and lay it all out: the bus, the soccer, Nonna’s days and Dad’s days.
And if she says yes, we celebrate with my tiramisu.
What about the three-hundred-dollar supply fee? That’s due with the acceptance form.
I’ll pay it online on Friday morning, once she’s decided. There’s no point paying before.
And whatever she chooses, I still want to see every drawing. Ashgrove or no Ashgrove, my kitchen table is still her studio.

qs.q: How does Graziella react to the news?
o: She is proud and not at all surprised.
She is worried about the long bus ride.
She thinks the school will be too demanding.
She wants Imogen to stay with her friends.
qs.ev: Of course she got in.
qs.x: “Of course” and her praise of Imogen’s drawings show pride and no surprise. The bus ride is Rhys’s concern.

qs.q: What is Rhys’s main concern at first?
o: The cost of the required art supplies
The very early morning bus departure
Imogen’s progress in core subjects
Imogen losing touch with her soccer team
qs.ev: My bigger concern is academics.
qs.x: He mentions the bus but calls academics his “bigger concern”, especially math. The supply fee comes up only at the end.

qs.q: Why do core subjects get the same hours at Ashgrove?
o: Art classes are held only twice a week.
The school day is longer than at other schools.
Students take extra math during the summer.
Art is taught during the lunch period.
qs.ev: They have a longer school day
qs.x: A longer day (8:30–3:45) makes room for two hours of art without cutting core subjects. Art is daily, not twice a week.

qs.q: How does Rhys respond to the information about test results?
o: He suspects the results are not accurate.
He still believes Imogen will fall behind.
He wants to see results from other years.
He is surprised and drops his main objection.
qs.ev: Okay, that takes away my main objection.
qs.x: “Huh … not what I expected” shows surprise, and he says his main objection is gone. He does not question the figures.

qs.q: Why does Graziella limit her offer to pick Imogen up?
o: She does not want to miss a regular activity.
She is no longer able to drive in the afternoon.
She thinks Rhys should take more responsibility.
She is worried that Imogen will be bored at her house.
qs.ev: I don’t want to give that up.
qs.x: Her aquafit class on Tuesdays and Thursdays matters to her, so she offers the other three days. Rhys volunteers on his own; she does not ask him to.

qs.q: What problem does the new school create for Imogen’s soccer?
o: Her team will have to play on Saturdays.
She will be too tired after the long ride.
She will not arrive in time for practice.
Ashgrove does not allow outside sports.
qs.ev: If she’s on a bus from Ashgrove, she can’t make it.
qs.x: Practice is at four at Glenwood, and the bus returns at 4:30, so she cannot get there. The Saturday league is a proposed solution, not the problem.

qs.q: Why does Rhys want Imogen to make the final decision?
o: He does not want to be blamed if it fails.
He thinks Valentina is pressuring her.
He expects her to choose soccer instead.
He feels she is old enough to weigh the costs.
qs.ev: She’s eleven, not five.
qs.x: He believes an eleven-year-old can understand the trade-off and that her choice will be meaningful. Nothing suggests he expects her to pick soccer.

qs.q: When will the supply fee be paid?
o: Tonight, after the family talks with Imogen
Once Imogen has made up her mind
Immediately, to secure her place at Ashgrove
On the first day of the new school year
qs.ev: I’ll pay it online on Friday morning, once she’s decided.
qs.x: Valentina will pay on Friday after Imogen decides; there is “no point paying before”. The talk is tonight, but payment waits.

parts.context: You will hear a report about whether children should repeat a grade at school.

lines: Each June, a small number of Canadian parents receive a difficult phone call: their child’s teacher is recommending that the child repeat a grade. It’s a practice that has fallen out of favour in many school boards, but it has never disappeared, and some parents are now asking for it themselves. Clara Montague’s son repeated Grade One three years ago, at her request. She says it was the best decision she ever made. He was the youngest in his class, he couldn’t yet read simple words, and he cried every morning. The second time around, she says, he was one of the strongest readers in the room, and his confidence returned. Stories like hers explain why the idea remains popular with many parents and some teachers. They argue that moving a child ahead before he’s ready, a practice critics call social promotion, simply passes the problem to the next teacher, with the gap growing every year. But researchers urge caution. Dr. Anand Venkataraman has reviewed decades of studies on the subject.

What we see in the research is quite consistent. In the first year after repeating, children often do look better, because they’re now being compared with younger classmates and they’ve seen the material before. But three or four years later, that advantage has usually disappeared. And among students held back, especially after Grade Three, we see higher dropout rates in high school. I’m not saying retention never helps an individual child. I’m saying it’s a very blunt tool, and we tend to remember the success stories. The children for whom it didn’t work are much harder to see, because their difficulties often show up years later, long after anyone connects them to that decision. So when a parent asks me, I always ask a second question: what exactly will be different the second time around?

Dr. Venkataraman argues that the real choice isn’t between holding children back and simply moving them along. Several boards are now trying a third approach: children move up with their classmates, but with a detailed support plan, which may include a summer reading program, small-group instruction or extra time with a specialist. Early results are promising, but these programs cost money, and many schools have waiting lists for exactly the specialists they depend on. Teachers’ groups say this is the weakness of the middle path. Without guaranteed funding, they warn, promotion with support can quietly become promotion without it. For parents like Clara Montague, that is the heart of the matter. If the support had been there, she told us, she might have chosen differently. But it wasn’t, and she couldn’t bear to watch her son struggle for another year.

qs.q: Why did Clara Montague ask for her son to repeat Grade One?
o: His teacher had strongly recommended it.
He had missed several months of school.
He was struggling with learning and with his emotions.
He wanted to stay with his younger friends.
qs.ev: he couldn’t yet read simple words, and he cried every morning
qs.x: He could not read and cried every morning, so he was struggling academically and emotionally. It was at her request, not the teacher’s recommendation.

qs.q: What do supporters of repeating a grade say about “social promotion”?
o: It leaves learning gaps that widen over time.
It is the main cause of high school dropouts.
It costs boards more than holding students back.
It is used mostly for the youngest students.
qs.ev: simply passes the problem to the next teacher, with the gap growing every year
qs.x: Supporters say promotion passes the problem on and the gap grows every year. Higher dropout rates are linked by the researcher to retention, not promotion.

qs.q: According to Dr. Venkataraman, why do students who repeat a grade often seem to improve at first?
o: They receive extra help from specialists.
Their parents become more involved.
They are more motivated the second time.
They are older and already know the content.

p1.meta: From: Teresa Malinowski  |  To: Kasia Malinowski  |  Subject: Congratulations, and an offer
p1.text:
Dear Kasia,

Your mother called last night with the news, and I nearly dropped the phone. Congratulations on your acceptance to the nursing program at Bayview University! I know how hard you worked for those chemistry marks, and I’m so proud of you.

I’ll get straight to the point, because I know you have decisions to make. As you may remember, Piotr finished renovating our basement last fall. It now has a bedroom, a small bathroom and a kitchenette, and its own entrance at the side of the house. We had planned to rent it out, but we would much rather have you there.

We wouldn’t charge you rent. In exchange, we’d ask for a little help. On Tuesdays and Thursdays I work until six, and Piotr is often on the road, so someone needs to meet the girls at the school bus at 3:40 and stay with them until I get home. If you could do that, and walk Bruno on those days, we would consider ourselves more than paid.

I know residence has its attractions. You’d be on campus, close to your classes, and you’d meet people more easily. I was very lonely in my first year of university, living off campus, and I don’t want that for you. So please don’t feel you have to say yes for our sake. On the other hand, the bus from our house takes only twenty-five minutes to campus, and residence with a meal plan costs nearly fourteen thousand dollars a year. That is money you would not have to borrow.

There are a couple of house rules, mostly for the girls’ sake: no overnight guests on school nights, and we’d ask you to let us know if you’ll be out very late, just so we don’t worry. Otherwise, the basement is your space, and we won’t come down without knocking.

Your mother says the residence deposit is due May 1, so there’s no rush, but please let me know by then. And whatever you decide, Sunday dinner is at five, every week, for as long as you’re in the city.

With love and pride,
Aunt Teresa

p3.title: Lunch Lessons: Canada’s Push for School Food Programs
paras: For decades, Canada stood out among wealthy nations for one surprising reason: it had no national school meal program. While children in countries such as Finland and Japan have long eaten a free hot lunch at school, Canadian students relied on a patchwork of local initiatives, many of them run by volunteers and funded by charities, parent councils or individual principals. That began to change when the federal government announced dedicated funding to help provinces expand school food programs. Advocates welcomed the move but noted that the amount, spread across the country, works out to only a modest sum per child, far less than what many other countries spend. Provinces are expected to add their own money, and the size of those contributions varies widely.

Supporters point to a growing body of evidence that feeding students pays off in the classroom. Studies from several countries have linked school meals to better attendance and improved concentration, particularly in the morning. In one Canadian school district that introduced a free breakfast for all students, principals reported a noticeable drop in the number of students sent to the office before lunch. Teachers describe subtler effects as well. “Kids who wouldn’t touch a vegetable at home will eat a salad if their friends are eating it,” said one elementary teacher in Winnipeg. Researchers caution, however, that it is difficult to separate the effect of the food from the effect of the routine, the social time and the adult attention that come with a well-run program.

One of the fiercest debates concerns who should be fed. Targeted programs, which serve only children from low-income families, are cheaper, but they carry a well-documented risk: students may avoid the program rather than be seen as poor. Universal programs avoid that problem, since every child eats, but they cost considerably more, and critics question why public money should feed children whose families can easily afford lunch. Some schools have tried a middle path. At one Ottawa elementary school, meals are offered to everyone, and families pay what they can through an anonymous online system. The principal says roughly a third of families pay the full suggested amount, a third pay something, and a third pay nothing, and no child knows which group a classmate belongs to.

Practical obstacles remain significant. Many older schools were built without kitchens, so meals must be prepared off site and delivered, which raises costs and limits what can be served. Programs that depend on volunteers are vulnerable when those volunteers burn out or when their own children move on to high school. Food waste is another concern, especially when the menu does not reflect students’ cultural backgrounds. Perhaps the most overlooked problem is time. In many schools, the lunch period has shrunk to twenty minutes, and once students have lined up, washed their hands and found a seat, some have barely ten minutes to eat. Several nutrition experts argue that no program, however well funded, can succeed if children are rushed through their meals.

p4.title: Let Them Walk
p4.byline: Opinion | by Henrik Solberg, father of three and urban planner
p4.text:
Every morning at 8:20, the street in front of my children’s elementary school becomes a parking lot. Minivans idle in the bus lane, parents double-park to unload backpacks, and a crossing guard waves her arms at drivers who are, ironically, there to keep their children safe. A generation ago, most children in this neighbourhood walked to school. Today, according to the school’s own traffic survey, fewer than one in four do, and almost none walk without an adult.

I understand why. Parents today are bombarded with frightening stories, and no one wants to be the parent who took a risk and lost. But I want to suggest, as a father of three and a planner who has spent twenty years studying how people move through cities, that we have the risks almost exactly backwards.

The danger most parents fear, abduction by a stranger, is extraordinarily rare, and it has not increased in decades. The danger they actually face is traffic, and much of that traffic around schools is created by parents themselves. When hundreds of cars converge on one block in a fifteen-minute window, the children who are walking become less safe, not more. Every family that switches from driving to walking makes the street safer for everyone else’s child.

There are developmental costs, too. Walking to school alone, or with friends, is often a child’s first real experience of independence: choosing a route, judging when to cross, dealing with a small problem without an adult to fix it. Children who never practise these skills at eight or nine do not magically acquire them at fourteen. Teachers at my children’s school tell me that students who walk arrive more alert and settle into work faster, though I would not claim that walking alone explains this.

None of this means every child should be sent out the door on the first day of kindergarten. Readiness varies, and so do routes. A seven-year-old crossing one quiet residential street is not the same as a seven-year-old crossing a six-lane road. I am also aware that in some neighbourhoods, with no sidewalks or with real safety concerns, parents have good reasons to drive. The answer there is not to blame families, but to fix the streets.

That is where schools and cities come in. Schools can organize “walking school buses,” in which a rotating parent volunteer walks a set route and picks up children along the way, gradually handing over responsibility as children grow older. Cities can lower speed limits around schools, add crossing guards at the most dangerous intersections, and close the street directly in front of the school to cars for twenty minutes at the start and end of the day. Where such “school streets” have been tried, walking has increased sharply, and parents who were initially opposed have often become their strongest supporters.

Parents, finally, can start small. Walk with your child for a few weeks, then walk half a block behind, then meet them at the corner. Let them make the decisions while you are still close enough to help.

Our children are more capable than we give them credit for. The walk to school is one of the first places they can prove it.

t1.situation: Your child’s Grade 8 science group project counted for 20% of the term mark. Your child did most of the work because two group members did not contribute, but every member of the group received the same mark.
bullets: Explain what happened during the project
Explain why you think the marking was unfair
Suggest what the teacher could do
t1.model:
Dear Ms. Pereira,

I am writing about the water filtration project that my son, Elias, completed with his group last month. I want to begin by saying that he really enjoyed the topic and learned a great deal.

However, I am concerned about how the work was shared. Over three weeks, Elias built the prototype, ran the tests and wrote most of the report. Two of his group members missed both planning meetings and contributed only one slide each. He asked them several times, and I have seen the messages. In the end, all four students received the same mark of 72%.

Since the project is worth 20% of the term mark, this feels unfair, both to Elias and to the students who did contribute. More importantly, I worry that he has learned that effort does not matter.

Would you consider asking each student to submit a short reflection describing their own contribution? Many teachers also use peer evaluations to adjust individual marks. I would be grateful if this could be applied to future projects as well.

Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
Noor Halabi

t2.intro: Your employer can afford to offer one new benefit to all employees and has asked staff to vote on which one it should be.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: Tuition reimbursement: up to $3,000 per year for job-related courses, certificates or degrees.
t2.b: Child care support: up to $3,000 per year toward licensed child care or after-school programs for employees with children under 13.
t2.model:
Although both benefits are valuable, I prefer Option A, tuition reimbursement.

My main reason is that it is open to every employee. Child care support would only help staff with young children, which in our company is probably less than a third of us. Tuition reimbursement, on the other hand, could help a new graduate earn a professional certificate, a mid-career employee learn new software, or an older worker retrain before retirement. A benefit paid for by the company should be available to as many people as possible.

Second, education benefits the company as well as the employee. When staff upgrade their skills, they become more productive, and they are more likely to stay. Training new hires is expensive, so keeping experienced people saves money in the long run.

I fully understand that child care costs are a heavy burden for young families, and I sympathize with my colleagues who are parents. However, many of them already receive government subsidies, and they could also use tuition reimbursement to build their careers.

For these reasons, I believe Option A is the fairer and more useful choice.

t1.prompt: Your friend’s elderly parents want to move into her home. She has two teenagers and a small house, and she works full-time. Advise your friend about how to approach this situation.
t1.model: Oh, that’s a big decision, and I can tell you’re torn about it. Before you say yes or no, I’d take a few weeks to think it through properly. First, have a really honest conversation with your parents about why they want to move in. Is it about money, loneliness, or their health? Because the answer changes everything. If it’s mainly loneliness, maybe a smaller apartment nearby would work better. If their health is declining, you need to think about who will look after them while you’re at work all day. Second, talk to your teenagers. Giving up a bedroom or sharing a bathroom with grandparents is a big change at their age, and they’ll cope much better if they feel included in the decision. Third, look at your house realistically. Could you turn the basement or the den into a bedroom with some privacy? Even a small renovation might make a huge difference. And if you do go ahead, set some ground rules from the start, like who pays for groceries, and whether your parents will help with cooking or rides. Finally, agree on a trial period, maybe six months, so everyone knows it can be reviewed. That makes it much easier to talk openly if it isn’t working.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you struggled with a subject at school. What happened, and how did you deal with it?
t2.model: In Grade Eleven, I really struggled with chemistry. I’d always done well in science, but suddenly we were balancing equations and calculating moles, and I just couldn’t follow it. On my first test, I got fifty-three percent, and I was devastated. I remember hiding the test in my backpack so my parents wouldn’t see it. Eventually, though, I realized hiding it wouldn’t help. I went to my teacher, Mr. Lacroix, and asked for extra help. He suggested I come to his classroom at lunch twice a week, and he explained things using cooking examples, like following a recipe, which suddenly made sense to me. I also started studying with a friend who was good at math. By the end of the semester, I had a seventy-eight. More importantly, I learned that asking for help isn’t a sign of weakness.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the mother with the stroller and the little boy will finish crossing the street safely, and the boy will run over to the father who’s waving beside the blue car. They’ll probably put his backpack in the trunk and drive home. Once everyone is across, the crossing guard will lower her stop sign and step back onto the sidewalk so the cars can move again. Meanwhile, the two kids with backpacks will climb onto the school bus, and the driver will probably wait a few more minutes for any other students who are running late. I also think the little dog might get excited when it sees all the children and start barking or pulling on its leash, and a couple of kids will stop to pet it. In about ten minutes, the street will be quiet again.

t5.intro: You are starting college in the fall and need to decide where to live. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

other.title: Living at home
details: 1 hour 15 minutes each way by transit

t5.persuade: Your parents prefer that you live at home. Persuade them that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know living at home would save us a lot of money, and I really appreciate that you’d keep my room for me. But I think the residence is the better choice, at least for first year. First, look at the commute. An hour and fifteen minutes each way is two and a half hours a day on transit. That’s over twelve hours a week I could be studying or sleeping, and my nursing labs start at eight. Second, the first year is when people make friends and join study groups. If I’m always rushing for the last bus, I’ll miss all of that. Yes, residence costs more, but meals are included, so I won’t be eating fast food on campus every day. And it’s only five minutes from class. Let me try residence for one year, and if it’s too expensive, I’ll move back home.

t6.situation: You are a member of your child’s school parent council. You have noticed that the council treasurer, who is a good friend of yours, has kept the cash from three fundraisers at home for several weeks instead of depositing it in the bank, as the council’s rules require. The total is about $2,400, and other members have started asking questions.
options: Talk to the treasurer and ask her to deposit the money immediately.
Talk to the council chair and explain what you have noticed.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hey, Lucinda, have you got a minute? This is a bit awkward, so I’ll just say it. I noticed that the money from the bake sale, the movie night and the book fair still hasn’t been deposited. I know how busy you’ve been with your mom in the hospital, and I’m not suggesting anything is wrong. But our rules say deposits have to be made within a week, and some of the other parents have started asking questions at meetings. I really don’t want anyone to get the wrong idea about you. Could we go to the bank together tomorrow morning? I can pick you up at nine, and we’ll get it done in fifteen minutes. And if the treasurer job is too much right now, maybe we could ask someone to share it with you for a few months.

t7.prompt: Answer the following question: Should parents strictly limit how much time their teenagers spend on screens? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: In my opinion, parents should set some limits on teenagers’ screen time, but strict limits usually don’t work, and they can actually damage the relationship. First, I think a few clear rules are necessary. Research shows that screens in the bedroom at night really affect teenagers’ sleep, and sleep is essential for their mood and their marks. So a rule like “all phones charge in the kitchen after ten p.m.” makes a lot of sense, and it’s easy to enforce. Similarly, no phones at dinner is reasonable, because family time matters. However, strictly limiting teenagers to, for example, one hour a day isn’t realistic. Teenagers use screens for homework, for group projects and to stay in touch with friends, and much of their social life happens online now. If parents are too strict, teens will simply hide what they’re doing, and parents lose the chance to guide them. My cousin’s parents banned social media completely, and she just created secret accounts. Instead, I think parents should talk openly with their teenagers about how they use their devices, and gradually give them more independence as they show responsibility. After all, in a few years they’ll be adults managing this on their own, and they need to learn self-control now.

scene.alt: A college building with a large sign that reads TECH COLLEGE. On top of the flat roof, a red car is sitting completely upside down, with its wheels pointing at the sky. Below, a crowd has gathered on the sidewalk: a woman is pointing up at the car, a man is taking a photo with his phone, and a teenager is holding a map of the open house. A banner on the side reads OPEN HOUSE TODAY. There is a tree and a streetlamp nearby.

t8.prompt: Your brother’s sixteen-year-old son wants to become a mechanic. You walked past a college open house and saw this unusual display. Call your brother, describe what you saw, and explain whether you think his son should attend the open house. Your brother cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hey, you’ll never guess what I saw on my way home. I walked past the technical college downtown, and there was a red car sitting on top of the roof, completely upside down, with its wheels pointing at the sky. I honestly stopped in my tracks. There was a big blue banner saying “Open House Today,” and a whole crowd was gathered on the sidewalk, pointing and taking photos. A teenager was holding a map of the building, probably planning which workshops to visit. I asked someone, and apparently the auto mechanics students put it up there as a crane-lifting demonstration. I really think Mateus should go. If they can do something that creative, the program must be very hands-on, which is exactly what he loves. The open house runs until Saturday, so I could even take him.
